standard.title: Representations reflect contexts
standard.description: analyse how representations of people, places, events and concepts reflect contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain how current technology affects reading, creating and responding to texts (AC9E7LY01). They have not yet analysed systematically how representations across media reflect the contexts in which they are produced.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how representations of people, places, events and concepts in texts reflect the contexts in which those texts are produced.

nodes.label: Representations vary across contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how representations of people, places or events vary across texts from different contexts and explain what produces the variation.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two representations of the same person, place or event from different contexts (e.g. different publications, time periods or cultural positions) and describe how they differ.
nodes.typical_width: Examine how representations of public figures in media vary across different contexts — identifying specific differences in language, emphasis and framing, and explaining what contextual factors might produce them.
wider: Compare how a news event is represented in media from different national contexts, examining how national perspective shapes framing
Analyse how the same historical figure is represented differently across texts from different time periods, tracing how changing social values shape the representation

response_modes.reason: Students often treat representations as either accurate or inaccurate, missing the contextual logic that makes each representation coherent in its own terms. Multiple contexts — across time, culture, publication type — are essential for the insight that all representations are contextually positioned.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-contextual representation analysis is the heart of media literacy. The elaborations name public figures, news events and historical comparison as rich sites. Advancing students can develop genuine critical media literacy skills — understanding how context constructs representation rather than just noting differences.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least two representations of the same subject from different contexts
Student explains at least one contextual factor that produces the difference in representation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat representations as accurate-or-inaccurate (rather than contextually positioned) cannot analyse language features as context-reflective devices at N2 — the N2 analytical task presupposes representations are understood as constructed.

nodes.label: Analysing language features in context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how specific language features are used to represent individuals or groups in ways that reflect the text's context.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse how language features (e.g. word choice, grammar, framing) are used in a text to represent a person or group in a particular way, and connect the choices to the text's context.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse language features used across texts from different time periods to represent individuals or groups — identifying how language choices shift with changing contexts and what this reveals about the relationship between language and social values.
wider: Analyse how language that was normalised in historical texts to represent a group is recognised as problematic today, examining what this reveals about how contexts shape representation

Compare the representation of the same concept (e.g. 'progress', 'freedom') across texts from different political or cultural contexts, examining how the same word carries different representational freight

response_modes.reason: Analysing how language features reflect context requires students to integrate language analysis (specific features, choices) with contextual understanding (historical period, publication context, social values). These two competencies need to be coordinated rather than applied sequentially.

success_criteria: Student analyses specific language features (not just general register) used to represent a person or group
Student connects the language choices to at least one contextual factor — not just noting that the text is old or comes from a different culture
